article.title: GitHub's CTO Pledges Architectural Fix for Reliability, Then Actions Goes Down Again Six Days Later
article.summary: Days after CTO Vladimir Fedorov pledged to fix GitHub's scaling problems following a 7-hour-47-minute outage, GitHub Actions failed again for nearly three hours.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

GitHub's Chief Technology Officer Vladimir Fedorov published a blog post on August 20 pledging architectural changes to fix the platform's reliability problems, writing that "if you were trying to ship software that day, we let you down" about an August 17 outage that lasted 7 hours and 47 minutes, according to [The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/the-august-17-outage-and-the-work-ahead/). Six days later, on August 26, GitHub Actions failed again, with the code host's own incident report showing the disruption started at 1511 UTC, according to [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/devops/2026/08/26/github-actions-was-down-yet-again/5292679).

## What We Know

The August 17 outage disrupted GitHub Actions, pull requests, issues, Copilot, and APIs "as the platform failed to scale with demand," following an earlier Actions outage on August 6, according to [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/devops/2026/08/21/we-let-you-down-github-pledges-to-scale-up-before-developers-give-up/5291031). In his August 20 post, Fedorov wrote that "neither outage was caused by a code or configuration change," attributing both to capacity limits rather than a bad deployment, according to [The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/the-august-17-outage-and-the-work-ahead/).

Fedorov tied the failures to traffic growth, writing that monthly commits rose from 1.4 billion in April to 2.9 billion currently, alongside 24 million new repositories and 130 million merged pull requests each month, according to [The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/the-august-17-outage-and-the-work-ahead/). He said GitHub has "added more than 3 million CPU cores, 120 petabytes of high-speed storage, and significant network capacity," and that Microsoft Azure now "serves roughly 58% of GitHub's platform load and half of all Git operations, up from 12% of platform load in May," per the same post.

Fedorov committed to a specific architectural change: "Our next milestone is an architecture that scales read capacity linearly with the number of readers, enabling unlimited read operations," to be rolled out gradually "beginning with the largest monorepos," according to [The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/the-august-17-outage-and-the-work-ahead/). He closed the post with a pledge: "We'll earn your trust through the scaling and reliability of the platform."

That pledge was tested almost immediately. On August 26, GitHub Actions failed again after GitHub "identified an issue with a database primary and failed over to a replica, but said the move 'did not fully mitigate' the degradation," prompting the company to throttle inbound traffic while investigating "upstream Vitess issues" before gradually restoring service, according to [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/devops/2026/08/26/github-actions-was-down-yet-again/5292679). GitHub said Actions was "operating as expected" again by 1800 UTC, putting the disruption at roughly two hours and forty-nine minutes. The Register noted the timing directly: "'We'll earn your trust through the scaling and reliability of the platform,' Fedorov wrote in last week's postmortem of the August 17 outage. Six days after he promised to fix things, here we are with reliability slipping and the issue count growing."

The August 26 incident left GitHub Actions at 98.13 percent uptime for the month, "nearly in danger of slipping into 97 percent reliability territory," according to [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/devops/2026/08/26/github-actions-was-down-yet-again/5292679). The outlet's review of GitHub's status-page history found the platform has logged at least 23 incidents every month in 2026, including 25 in January, 37 in February, 32 in March, 26 in April, 23 in May, 23 in June, 26 in July, and 23 in August with several days still left in the month. GitHub did not respond to The Register's request for comment on the August 26 incident.

## What We Don't Know

GitHub has not said when its linear-read-scaling architecture will roll out beyond "the largest monorepos" first, or given a timeline for reaching the rest of its infrastructure. It is also not yet clear whether the August 26 database-primary failure is connected to the capacity issues Fedorov described in his August 20 post, since that post predates the incident. GitHub has not published a separate detailed postmortem for the August 26 outage beyond its incident-report language cited by The Register.

## Analysis

The six-day gap between Fedorov's public commitment and the next Actions failure underscores the gap between GitHub's stated remediation — added CPU cores, expanded storage, and a shift of load onto Azure — and the platform's day-to-day reliability, as previously reported when [an eight-hour Actions outage in early August](/article/2026-08/07-github-actions-outage-spans-over-eight-hours-cascading-into-pages-copilot-and-webhook-delivery) extended a run of dozens of monthly incidents, and when [Cursor's rival Origin hosting platform launched the same day as the August 17 outage](/article/2026-08/19-cursor-launches-origin-code-hosting-platform-then-watches-a-six-hour-github-outage-hit-it-on-day-one). GitHub Actions sits at the center of many teams' CI/CD pipelines, so each disruption to the service has an outsized effect on software delivery beyond GitHub's own reliability metrics.
